headline: Prices for a typical Vaughan home are about 5% lower than a year ago, and condo apartments are down about 6.5%. The Bank of Canada raised its rate to 2.5% on October 28, which keeps borrowing costs from falling. Few new towers are starting, so the VMC is in a slow, wait-and-see stretch.

status.label: Fewer new homes under way
status.explanation: Vaughan had 3,144 homes under construction in September, down from 3,588 a year ago and far below the peak of 9,815. Only 1,243 homes have started so far in 2026. Many towers finished in 2025 (6,368 completions). The VMC census tract recorded 673 starts so far this year. Across the GTHA, pre-construction and under-construction condo inventory is down 37% from a year earlier.

status.label: Weak jobs, steady resales
status.explanation: Ontario's unemployment rate rose to 7.3% in October, and employment was little changed for a third month. Fewer jobs can mean fewer new buyers and renters. In Vaughan, resale activity continues: 263 sales in October, with 4.8 months of inventory.

status.label: Prices still drifting lower
status.explanation: The typical Vaughan condo apartment is priced at $504,900, down 6.5% from a year ago and about 42% below its March 2022 peak of $864,400. Buyers paid about 97% of the asking price in October. These are Vaughan-wide figures; the VMC is mostly condo apartments.

status.label: Rents flat to slightly lower
status.explanation: Average rent in the Richmond Hill/Vaughan/King zone was $1,726 in 2025, down from $1,762 in 2024. Vacancy was 2.4%. This is a wider zone than the VMC. CMHC says rental conditions are expected to continue easing.

status.label: Plans are big, starts are slow
status.explanation: There are 89 active development applications, with about 17,363 homes proposed in active site plans. But no new applications arrived in the last 180 days, and the GTA presale market is very weak: only 50 pre-construction condo sales in the GTHA in the second quarter.

personas.bottom_line: Prices are lower than a year ago, but borrowing costs are not falling.

points.text: A typical Vaughan condo apartment costs $504,900, about 6.5% less than a year ago.
The Bank of Canada raised its rate to 2.5%. The posted 5-year mortgage rate is 6.19%, a little higher than a year ago. Posted rates are higher than most negotiated rates.
Buyers of new condos in the GTHA often paid well below the asking price, and developers hold a record number of finished, unsold units.

personas.bottom_line: Rents are not rising fast, and there is more choice than a few years ago.

points.text: Average rent in the Vaughan area zone was $1,726 in 2025, lower than $1,762 in 2024. Vacancy was 2.4%.
CMHC says rental conditions are expected to continue easing, but slowing condo completions will place renewed pressure on rents in coming years.
Condo completions in Vaughan were 6,368 in 2025, which added many possible rental homes. Starts have since slowed.

watch: Rental Market Survey results next year

personas.bottom_line: Family-sized homes are cheaper than a year ago, but the economy is soft.

points.text: A typical Vaughan townhouse is $714,500 (down 8.9% in a year). A typical detached home is $1,482,000 (down 5.4%).
Ontario's unemployment rate was 7.3% in October, and employment has been flat for three months.
Mortgage rates are not falling: the Bank of Canada raised its rate on October 28 because inflation has been higher than expected.

personas.bottom_line: Sellers face lower prices and a market with plenty of choice for buyers.

points.text: Vaughan homes sold at about 97% of asking price in October, with 4.8 months of inventory.
A typical condo apartment has lost about 42% of its value since March 2022. Prices are still above the level of 10 years ago ($420,300).
There are 419 active condo apartment listings in Vaughan and 57 condo sales in October.
Developers hold a record 5,001 finished, unsold condos in the GTHA, which competes with resale listings.

personas.bottom_line: Rents are flat while prices are falling, so the numbers are tight and the risks are real.

points.text: Average rents in the wider zone were $1,726 in 2025, with vacancy at 2.4%.
GTHA new condo sales rose in the second quarter, but included some large bulk sales to investment groups. Pre-construction sales fell 80%.
Borrowing costs are not falling: the policy rate rose to 2.5% and the posted 5-year mortgage rate is 6.19%.

personas.bottom_line: Selling a bigger home may bring less than in 2022, while condo prices are also lower.

points.text: A typical Vaughan detached home is $1,482,000, down 23% from its June 2022 peak of $1,926,600.
A typical condo apartment is $504,900, so the gap between a house sale and a condo purchase is still large.
There are many condo listings (419 active in October) and new buildings keep finishing, so there is choice.

watch: Fees and costs in new buildings

scenarios.name: optimistic
scenarios.summary: Prices stabilise and new building restarts as costs and fees come down.

assumptions.assumption: Stays at or below 2.5% through 2027, with no further hikes.
Cuts to development charges under the Ontario-federal deal reach builders and lower project costs.
Ontario unemployment falls back below the 7.0% level by late 2027.

drivers.text: A deal to cut development charges in half for three years could make some projects pay off again.

scenarios.name: base
scenarios.summary: Prices drift sideways to slightly lower, new starts stay low and the VMC grows slowly.

assumptions.assumption: Stays near 2.5% for most of 2027, as inflation is projected to stay around 3% through much of 2027.
Starts over the next 12 months stay near 1,000 to 2,500 homes, not back to the 2021 level of 5,564.
Average rent in the Vaughan zone stays below $1,800 a month in the next survey.

drivers.text: Higher-for-longer interest rates keep buyers cautious.
A large pipeline of proposals (89 active applications) keeps the long-term plan alive.

scenarios.name: pessimistic
scenarios.summary: Weak jobs and more rate hikes push prices lower and delay more projects.

assumptions.assumption: Rises above 2.5% in 2027 because inflation stays high.
Ontario unemployment stays at or above 7.3%.
Developers keep holding record unsold finished condos (5,001 units in the GTHA in Q2) and pre-construction sales stay near 50 units a quarter.

drivers.text: Weak jobs and a higher policy rate hurt buyers.
Under-construction units already fell to 3,144 from 3,588 a year ago.

baseline_views.reason: Prices are falling about 5% a year, and the Bank of Canada raised its rate on October 28. The baseline already allows for this.
No strong evidence to depart from the baseline. Weak jobs and higher rates push down; cheaper development charges and a thinning pipeline push up later.
Condo prices are falling about 6.5% a year with record unsold finished condos around the GTA, but sellers are not cutting faster. In line with the baseline.
The baseline expects a mild decline. Evidence is mixed: a thinning pipeline helps later, weak presales and jobs hurt now.
Starts are low (1,243 so far in 2026) and presales are very weak. Development charge cuts may help later, so the baseline is reasonable.
Apartment starts follow condo presales, which are very weak. The baseline range is very wide because past errors were large.
Completions are outpacing starts, so the number under construction is drifting down (3,144 vs 3,588 a year ago).
CMHC says rental conditions are expected to continue easing, after average rent fell in 2025. Slowing completions could add pressure later.

events.title: Ontario and Ottawa announce $8.8 billion to cut development charges
events.impact: The announced deal aims to cut development charges in half for three years. Whether Vaughan takes part is not confirmed in the sources reviewed. Lower fees could help new towers pay off.

events.title: Urbanation: GTHA new condo sales rise for the first time in three years
events.impact: Sales were 702 units in Q2, but included some large bulk sales to investment groups. Pre-construction sales fell 80% to 50 units, so new towers still struggle to launch.

events.title: Bank of Canada raises its rate to 2.5%
events.impact: The bank raised its policy rate by 0.25 points. It said inflation has been higher than anticipated and is projected to stay around 3% through much of 2027. That keeps mortgage costs from falling.

events.title: Ontario unemployment rises to 7.3%
events.impact: Employment was little changed for a third month. Weak jobs can reduce buyer confidence.

watch_list.threshold: Next decision is December 9, 2026. A second hike would be a negative sign; a pause would mean steady costs.
watch_list.why: Mortgage rates drive what buyers can afford.
It would show the price slide is ending.

watch_list.threshold: Above 6 months means buyers have the upper hand; below 4 means sellers do.
watch_list.why: It shows how balanced the resale market is (4.8 in October).
It shows whether new supply is thinning faster.

watch_list.threshold: Moving well above 50 units a quarter
watch_list.why: New towers need presales to launch.

watch_list.threshold: Staying at or above 7.3%, or falling under 7%
Any new applications after none in 180 days
